description:
Section A — Key Material Lifecycle.

BearerAuth and BasicAuth at crate-jmap-base-client/src/auth.rs:151-245 store credentials in a plain String header_string field:

- BearerAuth.header_string = format!("Bearer {token}")
- BasicAuth.header_string = format!("Basic {base64(user:pass)}")

String::drop deallocates the buffer back to the allocator but does NOT overwrite its contents. The credential bytes remain in process memory until the allocator returns the slab and reuses it. A core dump (panic, OOM kill, attached debugger, /proc/PID/mem) recovered while or shortly after the JmapClient is dropped will yield the literal credential text.

The workspace AGENTS.md explicitly calls this out ("Section A — KEY MATERIAL LIFECYCLE" in the /review-crypto-security prompt; the workspace-wide rule says 'Secrets are zeroized on drop. In Rust: Zeroize or ZeroizeOnDrop'). The existing tripwire tests (bearer_auth_debug_does_not_leak_token, log_redaction.rs) defend against the in-life-time leak via Debug/tracing. They do not defend against the after-life-time leak via core dump / process memory inspection.

# What goes wrong (key recovery)

A core dump or live-process memory inspection on a long-running JMAP client process recovers the Authorization header bytes. The bytes are well-formed and immediately usable: the attacker copies the 'Bearer xyz...' or 'Basic abc...' string and replays it against the JMAP server. There is no key-derivation chain to walk; the recovered bytes ARE the credential.

# Suggested fix

Two layers:

1) Add zeroize 1.x as a dependency. Wrap header_string in zeroize::Zeroizing<String> or derive ZeroizeOnDrop on the structs. Both BearerAuth and BasicAuth get the same treatment.

2) For BasicAuth, the intermediate format!("{username}:{password}") String built before base64-encoding ALSO needs zeroizing. Currently at line 224 a fresh String is built, base64-encoded, then dropped — that String is the most attack-relevant artifact because it carries the plaintext password (the encoded form is recoverable by decoding the base64, but the plaintext form is one less step). Use a Zeroizing<String> for the intermediate.

3) Bonus: the caller-supplied &str token in BearerAuth::new is outside the type's control; document at the AuthProvider trait level that callers SHOULD provide tokens via Zeroizing<String> or equivalent.

# Pushback / why this might be P3 not P2

In a single-user CLI tool, the credentials are also in argv, environment variables, the shell history file, and possibly a .netrc — many places more exposed than process heap. For server-side multi-tenant deployments (which is the real consumer base for this kit per the workspace AGENTS.md kit/consumer split), each tenant's credentials are held for the lifetime of the request handler; cross-tenant memory contamination via allocator reuse is the realistic threat. P2 is the conservative read.

# Test discipline

zeroize crate does not provide a runtime tripwire for 'this field was zeroized after drop' — you'd have to instrument the Drop path or use unsafe with a probe allocator. The defensive value is in the discipline and the derived contract, not in a regression test. Document the constraint in the AuthProvider trait rustdoc.

# References

- zeroize crate documentation
- secrecy crate (alternative wrapper pattern with stricter access discipline)
- Workspace AGENTS.md 'Security testing' section (Pattern 1 covers Debug; this finding extends to drop-path discipline)
title: BearerAuth/BasicAuth credentials are not zeroized on drop; reside in freed heap until allocator reuse
